beats.text: Nine months before Rosa Parks, she refused to move.

overlays.hook: Nine months before Rosa Parks, *she refused to move.*

beats.text: On March 2, 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, she was fifteen, riding the bus home from school.
The driver told her to give up her seat to a white woman. She stayed put.
She said it was her constitutional right to sit there.
Two police officers pulled her off the bus in handcuffs. She spent hours in jail before her minister paid her bail.

visual.caption: Segregated waiting room, Durham, North Carolina, 1940

beats.text: Civil rights leaders chose not to build their fight around her. She was a teenager, and soon pregnant.
Nine months later, Rosa Parks was arrested, and the bus boycott began.
But in 1956, Claudette became one of four plaintiffs in a federal lawsuit, Browder versus Gayle.
They won. The Supreme Court upheld the ruling, and segregation on Montgomery's buses was over.
Her own arrest record stayed on the books until 2021, when a judge finally wiped it clean. She was eighty-two.
History remembers Rosa Parks. Claudette Colvin went first.

facts.claim: 2 March 1955, Montgomery, aged 15, riding home from school.
Refused the driver's order to give up her seat to a white woman.
Said it was her constitutional right to sit there.
Removed and handcuffed by two officers; hours in jail; minister paid bail.
Leaders/NAACP decided against her case: age and unwed pregnancy.
Rosa Parks arrested 1 Dec 1955 (nine months later); boycott began.
One of four plaintiffs in Browder v. Gayle (filed 1 Feb 1956).
District court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional (June 1956); Supreme Court upheld (Nov 1956).
Juvenile record expunged by Montgomery judge in 2021, aged 82.
